title: What Professor Aidarov Said
paragraphs: After every lecture, Kamila writes a short paragraph in her journal. Not a summary of the content, but a record of the most interesting things that were said — by the professor, by classmates, or by herself, in questions she asked. She has been doing this since her first week at WKU. "It forces me to paraphrase," she explains. "And paraphrasing forces me to understand. If I can say what someone said in my own words, I actually know it."

This week, the lecture was about language change — how languages evolve, borrow from each other, and sometimes disappear. Professor Aidarov began by saying that language was never static. He told the students that every generation changes the language it inherits, and that this is not decay but adaptation. He added that resistance to language change was itself a historical constant — every generation believes the next one speaks poorly.

"He said that the Kazakh language had absorbed thousands of Russian words over the twentieth century," Kamila wrote. "He said this was not a sign of weakness but of contact — and that contact between languages is usually a sign of contact between peoples. Then he asked us what we thought. He asked whether we found this reassuring or unsettling."

The discussion that followed was animated. One student said she thought borrowed words were a form of cultural contamination. Another said he believed languages had always borrowed from each other and that purism was impossible. Professor Aidarov told them both that they were partially correct. He explained that the tension between change and preservation was one of the central debates in linguistics.

"He told us to read Aitmatov," Kamila noted. "He said that Aitmatov wrote in both Kazakh and Russian — and that this was not a betrayal of either language but a bridge between them. He asked us to consider what it meant to write in two languages at once." Kamila wrote down the question and looked at it. She didn't have an answer.

Amir, who had been sitting beside her, leaned over and read what she was writing. "He also said something I found interesting," Amir told her afterwards. "He said that the most endangered languages in the world were not necessarily the smallest — sometimes large languages disappeared faster because their speakers became bilingual and stopped transmitting them to the next generation."

Kamila added this to her journal. At the end of the session, she counted the phrases she had recorded. There were eleven. Of those eleven, she had understood all of them immediately. Two years ago, she would have understood perhaps six. "Language changes," she wrote at the bottom. "So do I."

Reported speech, she realised, was more than a grammar exercise. It was a way of paying attention to what people actually said — not what you expected them to say, not what you wanted them to say, but what they actually said. "I think that's also what Aidarov was trying to teach us," she wrote. "Not just about linguistics. About listening."

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: What did you think of Aidarov's lecture today?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: It was excellent. He said language change was inevitable — that resisting it was always a rearguard action.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Yes. He also told us that borrowed words were signs of contact, not weakness. I liked that framing.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Did you notice he never told us what to think? He only asked questions. He asked what we found reassuring or unsettling.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: He said something about endangered languages too. That large ones could disappear if people stopped transmitting them.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Yes, and he told us to read Aitmatov. I've already started.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Good. I think we both understood why he said that — not just as reading homework.

keyPhrases.context: Paraphrasing forces you to understand what you've heard.
"Language was never static." — it always changes.
"Purism" = the belief that a language should be kept "pure" from foreign influences.
"The discussion that followed was animated." — lively, energetic.
"Speakers became bilingual" — they spoke two languages.
"Stopped transmitting them to the next generation." — passing language on.
Related to confirming or supporting someone's view.
"Resisting change was always a rearguard action." — fighting a losing battle.

vocab.definition: to express something using different words
vocab.example: Kamila paraphrases the lecture to check her understanding.
"Language was never static." — it always evolves.

vocab.definition: to receive something from a previous generation
vocab.example: Every generation changes the language it inherits.

vocab.definition: the process of making something impure by adding harmful or unwanted elements
vocab.example: "She thought borrowed words were a form of cultural contamination."

vocab.definition: the insistence on using only the original or "pure" form of a language
vocab.example: "Purism was impossible," said one student, because all languages borrow words.
The discussion was animated — everyone had a strong opinion.

vocab.definition: at risk of becoming extinct or disappearing
vocab.example: "The most endangered languages were not necessarily the smallest."

vocab.definition: to pass something on to the next person or generation
vocab.example: Speakers stopped transmitting their language to the next generation.

questions.text: Why does Kamila paraphrase lectures in her journal?
opts: Because she can't remember the exact words
questions.hint: "If I can say what someone said in my own words, I actually know it."

questions.text: What did Professor Aidarov say about language change?
opts: It is dangerous and should be resisted
It is natural adaptation, not decay
It only happens to small languages
questions.correct: It is natural adaptation, not decay
questions.hint: "He told the students that every generation changes the language it inherits, and that this is not decay but adaptation."

questions.text: The student discussion was quiet and uneventful.
questions.hint: "The discussion that followed was animated." — lively and energetic.

questions.text: Aitmatov wrote in both ___ and Russian.
questions.hint: "Aitmatov wrote in both Kazakh and Russian."

questions.text: What did Amir tell Kamila after the lecture?
opts: That endangered languages weren't always small
That Aitmatov was a bad writer
questions.correct: That endangered languages weren't always small
questions.hint: "He said that the most endangered languages in the world were not necessarily the smallest."

opts: Paying careful attention to what people actually say
questions.correct: Paying careful attention to what people actually say
questions.hint: "reported speech... was a way of paying attention to what people actually said."
"animated" = lively, energetic. An animated discussion = an active, engaged conversation.

questions.text: She ___ the lecture by writing the main ideas in her own words.
questions.hint: "paraphrase" = to express something using different words, showing you understood it.
"static" = not moving or changing. "Language was never static" = language always changes.
"endangered" = at risk of becoming extinct or disappearing entirely.
